purpose: Aminolevulinic acid is used in two main ways. In one form, it is applied to the skin to help treat rough, scaly skin patches called actinic keratoses, which are caused by sun damage and can sometimes turn into skin cancer. In another form, it is taken as a drink before brain surgery to help surgeons see and remove brain tumor tissue more clearly.
how_it_works: When aminolevulinic acid enters your body or is applied to your skin, it gets absorbed by abnormal or rapidly growing cells like cancer cells or damaged skin cells. Inside those cells, it turns into a substance that glows under a special blue or ultraviolet light. For skin treatment, a specific light is then shined on the area to activate it and destroy the damaged cells. For brain surgery, the glowing effect helps the surgeon tell apart tumor tissue from healthy brain tissue.
common_side_effects: For skin use: redness, burning, stinging, itching, peeling, or swelling at the treated area — these are very common and usually go away within a few days. For the drink used in surgery: nausea, vomiting, and your skin and eyes may become very sensitive to light temporarily.
warnings: Your skin will be extremely sensitive to light after treatment — avoid sunlight, bright indoor lights, and tanning beds for at least 48 hours after skin application or after taking the oral form. Going into the sun too soon can cause serious skin burns. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have a condition called porphyria, as this medication is not safe for those situations. The oral form is only given in a hospital setting under close medical supervision.
typical_dosing: For skin patches (Ameluz or Levulan): a healthcare provider applies the cream or solution directly to the affected skin area, waits a few hours, then uses a special light to activate it — usually done in one or a few sessions. For brain surgery (Gleolan): you drink a solution mixed with water about 3 hours before your surgery begins — the dose is based on your body weight and is prepared by your medical team.
